title: Supreme Court Justice Slams Arrests Over Chicken Biryani on the Ganga, Says 'Public Space for Dissent Is Shrinking'
excerpt: Justice Ujjal Bhuyan cites the Varanasi Iftar case to warn that ordinary activities are being criminalised and courts are failing to protect fundamental freedoms.
body:
• Supreme Court Justice Ujjal Bhuyan said consuming chicken biryani on the Ganga is 'not an offence' and criticised the arrest of youngsters who spent three months in jail for it
  • He warned that public space for expressing divergent opinions is shrinking in India and normal activities are being criminalised
  • The judge called out restrictive bail conditions that he said effectively discourage citizens from exercising their right to protest
  • He was referring to a Varanasi case where 14 people were arrested for eating non-vegetarian food during an Iftar party on a boat on the Ganga

Supreme Court Justice Ujjal Bhuyan delivered a pointed critique of the Indian judiciary's handling of protest-related cases on Saturday, warning that fundamental freedoms are under threat and that ordinary activities are being treated as criminal offences.

The Biryani Remark That Cut Deep

Speaking at the Justice GP Singh 4th Memorial Lecture at the National Law Institute University in Bhopal, Justice Bhuyan cited the Varanasi case in which a group of young people were arrested for eating chicken biryani during a Ramadan Iftar party on a boat on the Ganga river.

https://x.com/IndiaToday/status/2081354344017113426

"I am sure consuming chicken biryani is not an offence. It can't be an offence. There is no law prohibiting consumption of chicken over the Ganga river," Justice Bhuyan said. "They were arrested for that very reason and they had to remain in jail for three months."

The case drew national attention earlier this year when police in Varanasi charged 14 people under multiple sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, including promoting enmity, public nuisance, and outraging religious feelings. The complaint alleged that the group's act of eating non-vegetarian food on the river was "deliberately carried out to promote a jihadi mentality." The Allahabad High Court eventually granted bail after the lower courts had denied it, questioning whether the boatman's extortion allegations were credible.

A Wider Warning on Civil Liberties

Justice Bhuyan framed the biryani case as symptomatic of a broader erosion of constitutional protections. "It will not be an exaggeration to say that public space for expressing divergent opinion is shrinking in India," he said. "The right to express one's views and to demonstrate peacefully are fundamental freedoms of the citizens. Debate and dissent are the essence of democracy. Unfortunately, even normal activities are being criminalised."

"Citizens are finding that though the courts are responsive and do grant bail, do grant relief, many a times it is belated. But it is the restrictive conditions which are imposed while granting bail that are causing the greatest concern."

— Justice Ujjal Bhuyan, Supreme Court of India

He pointed to bail orders that direct accused persons not to attend public meetings, post on social media, or leave the country, arguing that such conditions effectively punish people for exercising their rights even after they are released.

The justice also referenced a Bombay High Court case involving a proposed solidarity demonstration for Gaza, saying he found it "very amusing" that a judge had questioned why people would want to protest over events outside India.

A Call to Universities

Justice Bhuyan called on universities to foster critical thinking rather than conformity. He said legal education should encourage students to question established norms, not merely repeat what they are taught. "I requested the university that allow the students to be themselves, encourage their inquisitiveness," he said.

His remarks carry particular weight coming amid the aftermath of India's student-led protest movement, which recently forced a cabinet reshuffle after weeks of demonstrations at Jantar Mantar. For the Indian diaspora, the speech underscores an ongoing debate about the state of civil liberties in the world's largest democracy — a question many carry with them wherever they live.
